stories.title: The August 17 outage, and the work ahead
stories.summary: On August 17, GitHub experienced an outage lasting 7 hours and 47 minutes that disrupted github.com, authentication, GitHub Actions, APIs, pull requests, issues, and Copilot. This was the second significant incident in August, following an Actions failure on August 6, and both were capacity failures triggered when critical infrastructure components failed to scale with peak traffic. The August 17 incident was worsened by a client-side retry loop in Copilot services that increased load during recovery. Since April, monthly commits have grown from 1.4 billion to 2.9 billion, intensifying pressure on the systems. In response, GitHub has added over 3 million CPU cores and 120 petabytes of storage while accelerating its migration to Azure, which now handles 58% of platform load, up from 12% in May. The company also plans to implement consistent retry limits, isolate critical systems, and remove shared dependencies to limit future outages.
stories.snippet: On August 17, GitHub experienced an outage that lasted 7 hours and 47 minutes. It disrupted github.com, authentication, GitHub Actions, APIs, pull requests, issues, and Copilot, affecting developers and organizations around the world. If you were trying to ship software that day, we let you down. This was our second significant incident in August, following an actions failure on August 6 . In March and April , I shared the work underway to improve GitHub’s reliability. We have made progress, but these incidents make clear that we must accelerate this work. What happened Our investigation found that the outage began when traffic reached a new peak, and a critical infrastructure component in our Central US data center failed to scale with it. The resulting capacity pressure spread through our systems, causing authentication failures and disrupting multiple GitHub services. Recovery required several coordinated actions. Teams rerouted traffic, isolated affected infrastructure, and restored services in stages. Most GitHub services recovered earlier that day, but some Copilot services took longer. stories.title: Supply chain attack on arrayref
stories.summary: On August 20, 2026, the Rust Security Response Team verified a report that the proc-macro1 crate was malicious, as its build script downloaded a harmful payload. Several crates—proc-macro1, proc-macro-en, aovine, arone, aronenao, and tinymember—were deleted from crates.io. The team also discovered that the popular arrayref crate had been republished to depend on this malicious crate, with its recent versions yanked. The malicious version was removed and the maliciously-yanked versions were unyanked, while other affected crates by the same author, internment and append-only-vec, received the same treatment and had their account locked. The author of arrayref is not believed to be acting maliciously, but their computer or credentials likely appear compromised, prompting users to verify their local dependencies.
stories.snippet:
What happened

On 2026-08-20 at 7:15 UTC we got a report that the proc-macro1 crate was malicious.

The Rust Security Response Team verified this to be the case: the crate had a build script that was downloading a malicious payload.

This crate proc-macro1 and others like it (proc-macro-en, aovine, arone, aronenao, tinymember) have been deleted.

Furthermore, we discovered that the popular arrayref crate had recently been republished and made to depend on this crate, with the most recent versions yanked. stories.title: GitHub Copilot app for Beginners: Managing your work
stories.summary: The GitHub Copilot app's "My work" pane provides a centralized location to manage pull requests and issues across multiple Copilot sessions. By default, it offers four views—All, Active, Review requests, and Done—with items automatically filtered to projects touched within the app. Users can create custom views by adding filters such as "Is: Issue" or "Assignee: Me," either typed out using angle-bracket syntax or built through the UI. Items display in either a list or table layout, with the table view allowing column customization, rearrangement, and resizing. From any item, users can launch new agent sessions using the issue as context, or select multiple items to bundle into a single session. Additional features include a repository filter scoped to touched repositories and a New issue button for creating issues directly within the pane.
stories.snippet: This is the third post in our GitHub Copilot app for Beginners series. If you’re just joining us, check out, GitHub Copilot app for beginners: Getting started , where we introduced the app and how it helps you work across multiple agent sessions. Our second post goes deeper on working within a session. Here, we’ll look at how to keep all of the requests and work being done on a project organized in one place. If you’ve been following along in this series, you know that real development is rarely a straight line. You fix a bug here, review a pull request there, and chase down a new idea somewhere in between. As you continue to assign tasks to Copilot and create new pull requests, you’ll quickly find yourself with several proverbial balls in the air. Being able to manage everything from one centralized location is key, and that’s exactly why the My work pane exists. Below, we’ll cover how you can use it to manage what’s currently in flight, what’s completed, and what’s next. stories.title: Announcing Rust 1.98.0
stories.summary: Rust 1.98.0 has been released by the Rust team and is available through rustup. The floating-point types f32 and f64 now include "algebraic" methods for addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and remainder, allowing compiler optimizations similar to -ffast-math, even though floating-point arithmetic does not strictly satisfy these algebraic properties. All primitive integer types now offer a format_into method that uses a NumBuffer to produce formatted strings, achieving performance comparable to itoa according to benchmarks. Additionally, the release updates the ManuallyDrop documentation to provide a stable guarantee that moving ManuallyDrop<Box<_>> after the box has been dropped will not be considered undefined behavior, addressing a long-standing compiler bug fixed in 1.96.0. These changes are detailed in the release notes for Rust, Cargo, and Clippy.
stories.snippet:
The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.98.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software.

If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, you can get 1.98.0 with:

$ rustup update stable

If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website, and check out the detailed release notes for 1.98.0.

If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel (rustup default beta) or the nightly channel (rustup default nightly). Please report any bugs you might come across!

stories.title: SPADE: Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments
stories.source: arXiv (Bo Liu, Simon Yu, Yiding Jiang et al.)
stories.summary: SPADE is a self-play reinforcement learning framework in which a single LLM plays two roles: an Environment Designer that writes complete, long-horizon training environments as executable code with an OpenAI Gym-style reset()/step() interface, and a Reasoning Agent that learns to act within them. Each environment is stateful and multi-turn, encompassing state transitions, reward functions, and verification code, so a single interface spans reasoning problems and multi-step agentic tool use. The Reasoning Agent's regret is estimated from the gap between its reward with and without privileged hints, which trains the Environment Designer to produce tasks at the edge of the agent's capabilities while keeping them feasible. Critical components include grounding the Environment Designer on documents sampled from a large pretraining corpus and providing it with an accumulated environment memory. Scaled to 30B-parameter models, SPADE improves over the strongest fixed-environment baseline by +5.3 on average across eight held-out math, science, code, and reasoning benchmarks, lifts tool-use by +5.7 on BFCL-v4 multi-turn and +13.9 on ACEBench-Agent, and yields growing margins in games as model scale increases.
stories.snippet: Continuous self-improvement requires an ever-expanding pool of self-generated, diverse, adaptive goals. For language agents, existing training environment pools (hand-curated, statically synthesized, or frozen-verifier) keep the goal distribution fixed as the learner scales. We introduce SPADE (Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments), a self-play RL framework in which a single LLM plays two roles: an Environment Designer that writes complete, long-horizon training environments as executable code with an OpenAI Gym-style reset()/step() interface, and a Reasoning Agent that learns to act in them. Each is a stateful, multi-turn environment (state transitions, reward functions, and verification code), so one interface spans reasoning problems and multi-step agentic tool use. The Reasoning Agent's regret is estimated using the gap between its reward with and without privileged hints; in optimizing this regret signal the Environment Designer learns to target environments at the edge of the agent's capabilities while keeping them feasible. stories.title: ADEPT: Accelerating Dexterity via Pre-Training and Post-Training using Reinforcement Learning
stories.source: arXiv (Jayjun Lee, Jessica Yin, Asif Rana et al.)
stories.summary: ADEPT is a large-scale reinforcement learning framework designed to learn sim-to-real transferable dexterity for high-DoF robot embodiments capable of solving long-horizon tasks from raw visuo-tactile perception. The approach pretrains a dexterous policy on a generic object reposing task, then post-trains downstream policies using this pretrained behavior as a prior, enabling new behaviors that are difficult to discover from scratch on multi-fingered robots. The pretrained policy zero-shots the reposing phase of downstream tasks, but naive RL fine-tuning rapidly degrades this capability, which the authors address with a stable post-training recipe combining behavior-cloning distillation, critic warm-up, and conservative on-policy updates. A joint-space Geometric Fabric is introduced to mediate between the RL policy and the robot, allowing safe exploitation of the full kinematic dexterity. The post-trained teachers are distilled into perceptive students that zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on two embodiments: a 23-DoF Kuka-Allegro with two RGB cameras, and a 29-DoF Flexiv-Sharpa with two RGB cameras and five vision-based tactile sensors, achieving human-level speed on challenging long-horizon tasks.
stories.snippet: We introduce Accelerating Dexterity via Pre-Training (ADEPT), a large-scale reinforcement learning (RL) framework for learning sim-to-real transferable dexterity across high degree-of-freedom (DoF) robot embodiments that can solve long-horizon tasks directly from raw visuo-tactile perception. ADEPT pretrains a dexterous policy on a generic object reposing task, then post-trains downstream policies with this pretrained behavior as a prior. ADEPT enables learning new behaviors that are otherwise difficult to discover from scratch on multi-fingered robots and avoids learning the same set of skills over again for every new downstream task. The pretrained policy zero-shots the reposing phase of downstream tasks, but naïve RL fine-tuning rapidly degrades this capability during transfer. We address this with a stable post-training recipe combining behavior-cloning distillation, critic warm-up, and conservative on-policy updates. To safely exploit the full kinematic dexterity, we introduce a joint-space Geometric Fabric that mediates between the RL policy and the robot. stories.title: Beyond Teacher Likelihood: Group-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation for Long-Context Reasoning
stories.source: arXiv (Zhu Zhang, Jixun Wang, Xiaoang Xu et al.)
stories.summary: The paper addresses a mismatch in on-policy distillation (OPD) for long-context tasks, where token-level teacher guidance can favor locally plausible responses that overlook evidence distributed across the input. The authors diagnose this teacher-verifier disagreement on two long-context evidence-aggregation benchmarks, finding that trajectory-level OPD scores become progressively less aligned with verifier rewards as input length grows. To address this, they introduce Group-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation (GC-OPD), which separately normalizes verifier rewards and OPD scores within each rollout group and computes a signed disagreement residual. A credit assignment method called RACA then distributes this residual across tokens based on their relative OPD advantages while preserving the original OPD signal. Experiments across five long-context benchmarks show GC-OPD raises Qwen3-4B's average score from 29.08 to 40.47 and Qwen3-8B's from 35.12 to 44.65, outperforming vanilla OPD which reaches 39.31 and 43.56. Ablations confirm that the signed residual is more effective than alternative calibration approaches.
stories.snippet: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own responses using dense token-level guidance from a stronger teacher. In long-context tasks, however, token-level teacher support can favor locally plausible responses that omit evidence distributed across the input or violate global task constraints. Task-specific verifiers, in contrast, evaluate task completion at the response level and may return graded rewards that reflect partial success. We diagnose this mismatch on fixed responses from two representative long-context evidence-aggregation tasks. Across longer input ranges, trajectory-level OPD scores become progressively less aligned with verifier rewards, indicating teacher-verifier disagreement. Motivated by this observation, we introduce Group-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation (GC-OPD). GC-OPD separately normalizes verifier rewards and trajectory-level OPD scores within each rollout group and uses their difference as a signed teacher-verifier disagreement residual. Relative-advantage-based credit assignment (RACA) distributes this trajectory-level residual across tokens according to their relative OPD advantages while preserving the original OPD signal. stories.title: Finetuning Strategies for Querying Sounds by Vocal Imitation
stories.source: arXiv (Aditya Bhattacharjee, Christos Plachouras, Sungkyun Chang et al.)
stories.summary: The paper "Finetuning Strategies for Querying Sounds by Vocal Imitation," authored by Aditya Bhattacharjee, Christos Plachouras, Sungkyun Chang, and Emmanouil Benetos, is a technical report describing their winning submission to the AES AIMLA 2025 Challenge on querying sound effects by vocal imitation. The authors investigate two complementary fine-tuning strategies for this task. The first approach employs contrastive learning with a frozen, pretrained CED encoder. The second utilizes joint contrastive-triplet learning with semi-hard negatives using a MobileNetV3 encoder. The report has been updated to include additional details released after the challenge. The work falls within the research areas of Sound, Artificial Intelligence, and Information Retrieval.
stories.snippet: This technical report describes our winning submission to the AES AIMLA 2025 Challenge on querying sound effects by vocal imitation. We investigate two complementary fine-tuning strategies: contrastive learning with a frozen, pretrained CED encoder, and joint contrastive-triplet learning with semi-hard negatives using a MobileNetV3 encoder. This report has been updated for posterity to include details released after the challenge.

stories.title: Lévy Attention: Single-Pass Predictive Uncertainty for Continuous-Time Attention
stories.summary: Continuous-time models for irregularly-sampled data (medical records, IoT streams, financial events) are increasingly common in production, but most systems can't afford the multiple forward passes that classical uncertainty methods like MC dropout require. Lévy Attention gives you a calibrated confidence score as a byproduct of the same forward pass that produces the prediction, with no extra sampling heads, ensemble members, or trained uncertainty branches to deploy. The accuracy cost of the operator swap is small, at most about 5.6% on the studied benchmarks and zero on the sparsest dataset, so engineering teams don't have to trade prediction quality for trust signals. The practical payoff shows up in serving: one pass ranks thousands of patients by trust in 1.4 seconds, and a split-conformal wrapper around the output hits nominal coverage at every level, meaning downstream systems can reliably route low-confidence predictions to human review. For engineers building healthcare, finance, or monitoring pipelines, this collapses the usual two-model pattern (predictor plus separate uncertainty estimator) into a single deployment unit, cutting latency, compute, and infrastructure complexity.
stories.snippet: Deep models for irregularly-sampled time series answer queries at arbitrary continuous timestamps, yet report nothing about how far each answer should be trusted. We show the attention layer itself can close that gap: with the right stochastic formulation, the pass that makes each prediction also reports, in closed form and at no extra cost, how far it should be trusted. We introduce Lévy Attention, a cross-attention operator whose output is a stochastic integral against an inhomogeneous Poisson random measure: query-key compatibilities assemble an intensity over a continuous (time x channel) index space, the measure scatters atoms under it, and the output averages an interpolated value field at those atoms. In expectation it reduces to a mollified cosine-kernel attention, so it replaces a softmax layer and trains with exact gradients. stories.title: Vomit: Clean up Claude 5's token output with a separate LLM
stories.summary: Vomit is a tool by zachahn that converts Claude's token output into English by piping it through a local LLM. It runs entirely locally with no telemetry and has no external dependencies. The project was vibe-coded and only tested on Mac, and the author notes it is pretty slow. Because the local LLM can only see what Claude tries to communicate and has no access to actions or files, it tends to hallucinate somewhat. There is also a possibility of completely missing Claude's message, in which case users can use AgentsView to retrieve the original messages. Vomit does not touch anything during runtime, except technically writing files to the user's TMPDIR.

stories.title: Feature Request: Support AGENTS.md
stories.summary: A GitHub feature request on the anthropics/claude-code repository proposes adding support for AGENTS.md, a unified Markdown file that coding agents can use to understand a codebase. The request, authored by DylanLIiii on August 21, 2025, notes that tools like Codex, Amp, and Cursor are beginning to standardize around AGENTS.md, while CLAUDE.md feels too specific to Claude Code and doesn't work as well when collaborating with developers who use other tools. The issue generated 373 comments and was labeled as an enhancement related to core functionality and memory. The issue has since been closed with the status marked as completed. Several related pull requests are linked to the discussion, including one merged pull request from another repository and multiple open and closed pull requests on the claude-code repository itself.

stories.title: Show HN: Omacosy – Omarchy-style tiling desktop for macOS, no SIP
stories.summary: Omacosy is a macOS desktop setup inspired by Omarchy that provides tiling window management using a real Super key and Hyprland's dwindle layout, all configured from a single GitHub repository. It includes a unified status bar process that handles the bar, popups, sliders, and screen dimming, alongside features like focus-follows-mouse, trackpad workspace swipes, a Mission-Control-style workspace overview with live previews, and focused-window border rings. The project ships with a theme-switching system that updates everything from the interface to the wallpaper in one step. Installation and uninstallation are automated via shell scripts, and a Brewfile is included for dependencies. According to the repository, the entire environment idles at roughly 157MB of memory, and it is organized into directories for binaries, configuration, helpers, patches, themes, and zsh configuration.

stories.title: Launch HN: Vendo (YC S26) – Let users build features on top of your product
stories.summary: Vendo is an open-source customization layer launched on Hacker News as a YC S26 startup, designed to let users build their own features and micro-apps on top of a host product. The platform is aimed at B2B SaaS teams whose customers frequently request bespoke features, functioning as an embedded agent that acts through the product's own API. The GitHub repository (runvendo/vendo) has garnered 502 stars and 74 forks, with 3,861 commits and active community engagement reflected in 36 open issues and 55 pull requests. The codebase is a TypeScript monorepo built with pnpm workspaces and Turbo, and includes a Claude plugin directory alongside documentation, examples, and scripts. Overall, Vendo positions itself as a way for product teams to let end users shape the software to their specific needs without requiring engineering work for every custom request.
stories.snippet:

stories.title: Aaron Swartz was prosecuted for scraping, while Meta does it without consequence
stories.summary: Aaron Swartz, one of the co-creators of the RSS protocol, was aggressively prosecuted for downloading approximately 70 gigabytes of academic articles from JSTOR and faced charges carrying up to 35 years in prison, a $1 million fine, and asset forfeiture. He ultimately took his own life rather than endure the court proceedings and impending financial ruin. Meanwhile, Meta torrented roughly 80 terabytes of books to train its AI models and faces little consequence beyond a likely financial penalty in court, with their AI models continuing to generate revenue. Swartz's actions were aimed at disseminating and archiving information for public benefit, while Meta's use of the same material powers proprietary AI systems that the author argues harm the environment and further enrich one of the world's richest people.

stories.title: Malicious Rust crate Arrayref runs a build-time payload
stories.summary: On August 20, 2026, a compromised release of the popular Rust crate arrayref appeared on crates.io, with version 0.3.10 added a dependency on a typosquatted crate called proc-macro1 whose build script downloads and runs a remote binary during compilation. The droundy maintainer account was compromised, and malicious versions of arrayref 0.3.10 and internment 0.8.7, along with append-only-vec 0.1.9, were published before being removed. A separate dtolney account impersonated David Tolnay to publish proc-macro1, whose source code was a genuine copy of the legitimate proc-macro2. The build script reassembled base64-encoded fragments to contact 23.254.165.112, fetched an architecture-specific binary over TLS with certificate validation disabled, and executed it detached. The attacker yanked older clean releases such as 0.3.9, leaving only the malicious 0.3.10 available.
